entry: Programming language for statistical computing and data visualization, widely used in data mining, bioinformatics and [[Data science|data science]]. Many software packages extend its core, including the tidyverse collection. R is free, open-source software distributed under the GNU General Public License, and is implemented primarily in [[C (programming language)|C]], [[Fortran]] and R itself. Ross Ihaka and Robert Gentleman developed it at the University of Auckland to teach introductory statistics, and in August 1993 posted a binary file of R on StatLib. It was inspired by the S programming language. Precompiled executables are available for [[Linux]], macOS and [[Microsoft Windows]].

Island in the Indian Ocean, an overseas department and region of [[France]] (pop., January 2026: 910,985). Known as Île Bourbon before 1848, it is part of the Mascarene Islands and lies 679 km east of [[Madagascar]] and 175 km southwest of [[Mauritius]]. Uninhabited before French settlement in the 17th century, the island developed a plantation economy focused on [[Sugarcane|sugar]]. Slaves from East Africa were imported as fieldworkers, followed by Malays, Vietnamese, Chinese and Indians as indentured laborers. [[Slavery|Slavery]] was abolished on December 20, 1848. Since 1946 the island has been governed as a French region, with a status similar to that of Metropolitan France, making it one of the outermost regions of the [[European Union]] and part of the eurozone. Réunion Creole is the predominant language, though French remains the sole official language. France maintains a large military presence on the island because of its strategic location.

[[Ancient Egypt|Ancient Egyptian]] deity of the Sun, identified primarily with the noon-day Sun. By the Fifth Dynasty, in the 25th and 24th centuries BC, he had become one of the most important gods in Egyptian religion, and he was believed to have ruled as the second pharaoh of Ancient Egypt. He usually appears as a man with a [[Falcon|falcon]] head beneath a solar disc with a cobra. Each day he carried the Sun across the sky in his solar barque; at night he traveled through the Duat (underworld), where the serpent Apophis attacked him in an attempt to stop his journey. In the New Kingdom he was fused with [[Amun]] as Amun-Ra, and at times he merged with [[Horus]] as Ra-Horakhty. The cult of the Mnevis bull, an embodiment of Ra, had its center in Heliopolis. In some accounts, humans were created from his tears and sweat.

Cuban politician and military leader, first secretary of the Communist Party of Cuba from 2011 to 2021. One of the military leaders of the [[Cuban Revolution]], he served as minister of the Armed Forces from 1959 to 2008. He became acting president in July 2006 during the illness of his brother [[Fidel Castro]], and was made president by the National Assembly in February 2008. He was re-elected in 2013 and stepped down as president in 2018, when Miguel Díaz-Canel succeeded him. He announced his retirement at the Eighth Congress of the Communist Party of Cuba in April 2021.

Capital city of Morocco, on the northwestern [[Atlantic Ocean|Atlantic]] coast at the mouth of the Bou Regreg, opposite Salé (pop., 2024: 515,619). It is the country's seventh-largest city and the second-largest metropolitan area after [[Casablanca]]. The name derives from the Arabic *ribat*, an Islamic fortification. Rabat was founded in the 12th century by the Almohads, who established it as a naval base in 1170. In the 17th century it became a haven for Barbary corsairs. The French made it the administrative center of their protectorate in 1912, and it became the capital when Morocco gained independence in 1956. One of the four imperial cities of Morocco, it has a medina that is a [[World Heritage Site]]. It hosts the headquarters of several international bodies, and the African office of [[FIFA]] and the regional office for the Maghreb of [[UNESCO]].

Jewish scholar and sage, a tanna of the latter part of the first century and the beginning of the second. He was a member of the Sanhedrin that determined the final canon of the [[Hebrew Bible]] and played a decisive part in the inclusion of the Song of Songs and Ecclesiastes, a canon later adopted by early Christian writers. A leading contributor to the Mishnah and to Midrash Halakha, he is referred to in Tosafot as *Rosh la-Hakhamim* ("Chief of the Sages"). According to the [[Talmud]], he was an uneducated shepherd employed by a wealthy citizen of [[Jerusalem]] until he married that man's daughter, and he began his studies at about age 40. He studied under Eliezer ben Hurcanus and Joshua ben Hananiah. He was executed by the Romans in the aftermath of the Bar Kokhba revolt.

Jewish preacher and religious leader, ordained by another rabbi through *semikhah* after study of Jewish history and texts, including the Tanakh, Midrash, Mishnah, Talmud and [[Halakha]]. The word derives from Mishnaic Hebrew *rabbī*, meaning "Master [Name]." The title was first used in the first century CE. The role developed between the Second Temple period and the Rabbinic period, when learned teachers codified [[Judaism]]'s written and oral laws. In more recent centuries, the duties of a rabbi became increasingly influenced by those of the Protestant Christian minister, and in 19th-century Germany and the United States, sermons, pastoral counseling and representing the community grew in importance. Ordination requirements differ among Jewish denominations, and non-Orthodox movements such as [[Conservative Judaism]] and [[Reform Judaism]] have set their own standards.

Small [[Mammal|mammal]] of the family Leporidae, which also includes the [[Hare|hares]], in the order [[Lagomorpha]]. The most widespread genera are *Oryctolagus* and *Sylvilagus*. The European rabbit, *Oryctolagus cuniculus*, is the ancestor of hundreds of domestic breeds and has been introduced on every continent except [[Antarctica]]. Although once considered [[Rodent|rodents]], rabbits have traits that rodents lack, including two extra incisors. They are nocturnal and have long hind legs for quick hopping, and their large ears aid [[Thermoregulation|thermoregulation]]. They breed quickly, with litters of four to twelve kits and no particular mating season. Humans have raised them as livestock since at least the first century BC in [[Ancient Rome|ancient Rome]], for meat, fur and [[Wool|wool]]. In some regions, especially Australia, they have caused ecological problems.

Viral disease that causes inflammation of the brain in humans and other [[Mammal|mammals]]. It is caused by lyssaviruses, including the rabies virus, and is usually spread when an infected animal bites or scratches another animal or a person; saliva that contacts the eyes, mouth or nose can also transmit it. Symptoms usually appear one to three months after infection, beginning with fever and abnormal sensations at the site of exposure, and then progress to violent movements, fear of water and confusion. Once symptoms appear, the result is virtually always death. [[Dog|Dogs]] are the animal most commonly involved globally, and rabies causes about 59,000 human deaths a year, with more than 95% of cases occurring in [[Africa]] and Asia. The rabies vaccine, sometimes with rabies immunoglobulin, prevents the disease if given before symptoms begin, and vaccination programs have reduced the risk from dogs in many regions.

Medium-sized mammal native to North America, the largest member of the family [[Procyonidae]]. Its dexterous front paws, facial mask and ringed tail are common themes in the mythologies of Indigenous peoples of the Americas. Raccoons are noted for their intelligence, and can remember the solution to tasks for at least three years. Usually nocturnal and omnivorous, it lives in forests, mountains, coastal marshes and [[Urban area|cities]]. As a result of escapes and deliberate introductions in the mid-20th century, raccoons now range across central Europe, the [[Caucasus]] and [[Japan]]. Life expectancy in the wild is only 1.8 to 3.1 years.

Categorization of humans into groups viewed as distinct within a society, based on shared physical or social qualities. The term came into common use in 16th-century [[Europe]] and the Western world for geographic and [[Kinship|kinship]] groups, often arranged in a hierarchy. Modern scholarship views racial categories as socially constructed: race is assigned by rules made by society and has no inherent physical or biological meaning, although it is partly based on physical similarities within groups. Researchers continue to disagree. Some argue that genomic data show continental-scale clusters, while others argue that race has no taxonomic significance because all living humans belong to the same subspecies, *Homo sapiens sapiens*. Since the second half of the 20th century, race has been associated with discredited theories of [[Racism|scientific racism]], and in 2023 the U.S. National Academies of Sciences, Engineering, and Medicine renounced its use in genetics.

American marine biologist, writer and conservationist. Her sea trilogy, beginning with *The Sea Around Us* (1951), which won a U.S. National Book Award, explored ocean life from the shore to the depths. In *Silent Spring* (1962) she turned to problems she believed were caused by synthetic [[Pesticide|pesticides]]. The book met fierce opposition from chemical companies, but it prompted a reversal in national pesticide policy, a nationwide ban on [[DDT]] and other pesticides, and a grassroots movement that helped lead to the creation of the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency. Supporters credit her with advancing marine conservation and the global environmental movement. Critics argue that she overstated some risks and that restrictions on DDT contributed to a resurgence of malaria, with estimates of excess deaths in the tens of millions. She was posthumously awarded the Presidential Medal of Freedom by President [[Jimmy Carter]].

American television news host and political commentator. She hosts *The Rachel Maddow Show*, a weekly program on MS NOW (formerly MSNBC). Her radio program of the same name aired on Air America Radio from 2005 to 2010. She has received multiple Emmy Awards, and in 2021 a Grammy Award for the audiobook of *Blowout* (2019). A Rhodes Scholar, she holds a bachelor's degree in public policy from [[Stanford University]] and a doctorate in political science from the [[University of Oxford]]. She is the first openly lesbian anchor to host a major prime-time news program in the United States.

Canadian actress known for film, television and theater work in comedy and drama. She rose to fame in 2004 with *Mean Girls* and *The Notebook*, and was nominated for the Academy Award for Best Supporting Actress for playing journalist Sacha Pfeiffer in *Spotlight* (2015). She appeared in the [[Marvel Cinematic Universe]] films *Doctor Strange* (2016) and *Doctor Strange in the Multiverse of Madness* (2022). She starred in the second season of the [[HBO]] series *True Detective* (2015) and made her Broadway debut in *Mary Jane* (2024), earning a Tony Award nomination. Her films have grossed over $3.4 billion worldwide.

British actress known for stage and screen performances. Her film breakthrough was as Evelyn Carnahan in *The Mummy* (1999) and *The Mummy Returns* (2001). She won the Academy Award for Best Supporting Actress for playing an activist in *The Constant Gardener* (2005), and a BAFTA Award for playing Sarah Churchill in *The Favourite* (2018), which earned her a second Academy Award nomination. For her portrayal of Blanche DuBois in a 2009 revival of *A Streetcar Named Desire*, she won the Laurence Olivier Award for Best Actress. She also appeared in the [[Marvel Cinematic Universe]] film *Black Widow* (2021).

Indian actress known for her leading roles in [[Kannada]]-language films. She made her feature debut in *Moggina Manasu* (2008), which won her the Karnataka State Film Award for Best Actress and the Filmfare Award for Best Actress – Kannada. Her commercial successes include *Hudugaru* (2011) and *Mr & Mrs Ramachari* (2014), which earned her a SIIMA Award. Her last screen appearance before a long break from acting was in *Aadi Lakshmi Puraana* (2019). She is married to actor [[Yash (actor)|Yash]] and endorses several brands.

Dimensionless [[International System of Units|SI]] unit of angle, the standard unit of angular measure in many areas of [[Mathematics|mathematics]]. One radian is the angle subtended at the center of a [[Circle|circle]] by an arc equal in length to the radius, so an angle in radians equals the arc length divided by the radius. A complete revolution is 2π radians, equal to 360 [[Degree (angle)|degrees]], and one radian is approximately 57.2958 degrees. The symbol is rad, although it is often omitted in mathematical writing, and angles without a stated unit are generally assumed to be in radians. The radian was formally recognized as an SI coherent derived unit in 1995. It is preferred in [[Calculus]] because the derivatives of [[Sine and cosine|sine and cosine]] hold without additional conversion factors only when angles are in radians.

Emission or transmission of energy in the form of waves or particles through space or a material medium. Radiation includes [[Electromagnetic radiation|electromagnetic radiation]], such as radio waves, microwaves, infrared, visible light, ultraviolet, [[X-ray|X-rays]] and [[Gamma ray|gamma rays]]; particle radiation, such as alpha, beta, proton and neutron radiation; acoustic radiation, such as sound and ultrasound; and gravitational waves. It is often categorized as [[Ionizing radiation|ionizing]] or non-ionizing according to the energy of the radiated particles. Ionizing radiation can knock electrons from atoms and break chemical bonds, damaging living cells and DNA, so exposure increases the risk of [[Cancer|cancer]]. Lower-energy radiation can cause vibrations in molecular bonds that are sensed as [[Heat|heat]]. Because radiation expands as it passes through space and its energy is conserved in vacuum, the intensity of radiation from a point source follows an [[Inverse-square law|inverse-square law]] with distance.

Treatment using [[Ionizing radiation|ionizing radiation]], generally as part of cancer therapy to kill or control the growth of malignant cells. Also called radiotherapy, it is normally delivered by a linear particle accelerator. Ionizing radiation damages the [[DNA]] of cancerous tissue, leading to cell death. To spare normal tissue, shaped beams are aimed from several angles to intersect at the tumor, giving a much larger dose there than in the surrounding tissue. Radiation therapy may be curative for localized cancers, may be used after [[Surgery|surgery]] to prevent recurrence, or may be [[Palliative care|palliative]]. It is often combined with [[Chemotherapy|chemotherapy]], hormone therapy or immunotherapy. Brachytherapy places a radioactive source inside or next to the area being treated. It is estimated that half of the 1.2 million invasive cancer cases diagnosed in the United States in 2022 received radiation therapy.

[[Atom|Atom]], [[Molecule|molecule]] or [[Ion|ion]] that has at least one unpaired valence electron. With some exceptions, these unpaired electrons make radicals highly reactive. Radicals are important in [[Combustion|combustion]], atmospheric chemistry, polymerization, plasma chemistry and [[Biochemistry|biochemistry]]. They can form by thermally induced fragmentation, by one-electron [[Redox|redox]] reactions, or by abstraction of a hydrogen atom from an organic compound; carbon–hydrogen bonds next to [[Ether|ethers]] and amines are especially susceptible. Absent steric bulk, a radical tends to form a bond by dimerization, so much of radical chemistry concerns stabilizing radicals. Electron-spin resonance uses microwave energy to flip the unpaired spin and reveals how radicals are bonded.

Transmission of signals, especially audio, to receivers using [[Radio wave|radio waves]] over a wide area. Terrestrial broadcasts from stations on land use analog AM or FM, or digital standards such as DAB (Digital Audio Broadcasting), HD Radio or DRM (Digital Radio Mondiale); audio is also broadcast by [[Satellite|satellite]]. Stations may produce their own programming or be affiliated with a network that supplies content through syndication or simulcasting. Early broadcasts transmitted [[Telegraphy|radiotelegraphy]], such as time signals and weather reports, and the U.S. Navy began broadcasting such signals in 1904. The first commercial broadcast took place on November 2, 1920, when KDKA in Pittsburgh aired the results of the Harding–Cox presidential election. In 1927 the Federal Radio Commission was established to manage interference and licensing.

Galaxy with giant regions of radio emission extending well beyond its visible structure, powered by jets from its [[Active galactic nucleus|active galactic nucleus]]. The radio emission is due to the synchrotron process, and the observed structure is determined by the interaction between twin jets and the external medium. Host galaxies are almost exclusively large elliptical galaxies. Because radio-loud active galaxies can be detected at large distances, they are valuable tools for observational cosmology. The term is often used for the entire jet system rather than only the host galaxy, and some scientists prefer "black hole jet system." Radio galaxies reaching about 0.7 [[Parsec|megaparsecs]] or more are called giant radio galaxies.

Specialized [[Antenna (radio)|antenna]] and receiver used to detect radio waves from astronomical radio sources. Radio telescopes are the main instrument of radio astronomy and, unlike [[Optical telescope|optical telescopes]], can be used in daylight as well as at night. Radio waves from celestial sources are extremely weak, so radio telescopes require very large antennas and extremely sensitive receivers. Most are parabolic dishes, used alone or linked in arrays, and observatories are located far from centers of population to avoid electromagnetic interference. Radio waves from space were first detected in 1932 by the engineer Karl Guthe Jansky at Bell Telephone Laboratories in Holmdel, New Jersey. The first purpose-built radio telescope, a 9-meter parabolic dish, was constructed by radio amateur Grote Reber in his backyard in Wheaton, Illinois, in 1937.

Type of [[Electromagnetic radiation|electromagnetic radiation]] with the lowest frequencies and longest wavelengths in the [[Electromagnetic spectrum|electromagnetic spectrum]], typically below 300 gigahertz (GHz). Radio waves travel at the [[Speed of light|speed of light]] in a vacuum and are generated by charged particles undergoing acceleration, such as time-varying electric currents. Natural sources include [[Lightning|lightning]] and astronomical objects, while artificial radio waves are produced by a transmitter connected to an [[Antenna (radio)|antenna]]. Their behavior depends on frequency: long waves diffract around mountains and follow the Earth's contour, shorter waves reflect off the ionosphere to return beyond the horizon, and much shorter waves travel along a line of sight. [[James Clerk Maxwell|James Clerk Maxwell]]'s theory of electromagnetism predicted them in 1867, and [[Heinrich Hertz|Heinrich Hertz]] demonstrated them in 1887. Their use is strictly regulated by the International Telecommunication Union to prevent interference.

Method for determining the age of organic material by measuring its radioactive carbon-14 (¹⁴C) content. Carbon-14 is constantly created in the atmosphere when [[Cosmic ray|cosmic rays]] interact with [[Nitrogen|nitrogen]], and it enters living organisms through [[Photosynthesis|photosynthesis]] and food. After an organism dies, its carbon-14 decays with a [[Half-life|half-life]] of about 5,730 years, so the oldest dates that can be reliably measured reach approximately 50,000 years ago. The method was developed in the late 1940s at the University of Chicago by Willard Libby, who received the Nobel Prize in Chemistry in 1960. Calibration curves convert measurements into calendar ages. Burning fossil fuels and nuclear testing in the 1950s and 1960s altered atmospheric levels, requiring further corrections. [[Mass spectrometry|Accelerator mass spectrometry]], which needs very small samples, is now the method of choice.
